source_refs.note: PDF 220 (book p. 218): 7.1.2 Vectors, definition and the examples displacement, velocity and acceleration

blocks.text: Vector quantities are described by both magnitude and direction.

items: Displacement: Displacement is change in position of a particle represented by a vector from initial to final position.
Velocity: Rate of change of displacement with respect to time in a specified direction (i.e., speed in a given direction). It is vector quantity and its magnitude gives speed.
Acceleration: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, including direction.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A vector needs two pieces of information: how much, and which way. "5 km" is a scalar; "5 km towards the east" is a vector.
Displacement looks only at the start and the end of the motion, not at the path in between: it is (final position) \(-\) (initial position). If you walk 3 km east and then 3 km back west, the distance is 6 km but the displacement is 0.
On a straight line, the direction is shown simply by a sign (this is explained in 7.1.3): with east as positive, \(+40\) m means 40 m east and \(-60\) m means 60 m west.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A vector has both magnitude and direction.
2. Displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors; distance and speed are scalars.
3. Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
4. The magnitude of velocity is speed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using distance where displacement is asked (or the other way round). If the particle turns back, the two are different.
2. Thinking a vector must be drawn with an arrow. On a straight line the sign \(+\) or \(-\) already gives the direction.
